Really fun game (better than Uplink). For someone who is sometimes oblivious to solutions that are right in front of them, Hacknet is pretty straight forward.

If you like hacking games, or are familiar with Unix/Linux systems, you'll love it.

My only other 'hacker' game I've played was Uplink so I will include comparisons with it.
Pros:
-There's a console where you use some linux commands like 'ls', 'mv', 'scp' and 'rm', so if this is the first time you use them, you get to feel the horror when you rm *
-The game really hits home the actual reality of gaining access to a system: maybe from brute force, maybe from exploits, but almost always from someone sending a password plain-text over an IRC channel or mobile device email.
-It's a bit more 'real' feeling than Uplink, due to the console, the irrelevance of geological locations, and the introduction of concepts such as 'ports', 'front ends', etc
Cons:
-The game is littered with a noticeable amount of spelling and grammar errors, enough that it doesn't feel like the developer planned to do it.
-It's still every bit as 'graphic' as Uplink; cracking a system consists entirely of executing programs that each crack their own type of port, and they all have their own little static animation they play.
-Most of the challenge comes when your 800ish MB of RAM isn't enough to execute them all when possible, and you have to wait for others to finish.

As for the story, I haven't finished it, so can't say.

If you really liked Uplink, or if you think you'd be really into a pretty simple Hollywood hacking simulator, it's an OK buy. I don't regret it.

This game is ace. It nails ridiculous hacker fantasy SO hard. This is every silly scene in a tech thriller where someone's furiously typing away and silly visualisers spin and animate while they break in to a mainframe. But within this there is a really compelling adventure game. The satisfaction of being given an objective and some vague pointers and then worming your way to the goal is brilliant, especially in the longer missions that can take you across a whole network. Hats off to all involved. They took a strong concept and followed through beatifully.

The game is a thoroughly fun exploration of a neat mechanic: "hacking" in a Unity command window. A lot of the visuals are very futurey-hacker cheesy, but it is still very endearing. The game is chock full of flavor and silliness, much of which is found by straying off the beaten path. The game ends before it becomes too crazy repetitive. For what came from a game jam, Hacknet developed itself into a cool, brief package that any computer-competent person can enjoy.

This game was a lot of fun.  Not a lot of hand holding -- just enough direction from emails and lessons to build you up to complete increasingly difficult challenges that revolve around a central story.

If you dabble in programming / mildly interested in computers, and want a simplified, engrossing hacking sim, this is for you.

The soundtrack is awesome too.
======== Other thoughts ===========
The hacking mechanics are gamified, but still based on real programs, attacks, and port numbers.  I've used a lot of command line, and muscle memory actually helped me in the game!  

While the game is built around *nix typed commands, some of them are less developed than their real world counterparts -- e.g. can't cd /arbitrary/path/to/directory, but it's game, so no complaints.
Extremely fun, good and funny references, very detailed and indepth in terms of "non-essential items" (i.e. like books in Syrim).  Overall a great game and extremely fun.

Probably the best spiritual successor to Uplink: Hacker Elite I've ever seen. As a hacking simulator it is fairly straight forward. You always know what to do and the challange lies in searching through logs and mails and "snoop around". Where Uplink had the greatest challange in hacking and cracking Hacknets hacking is pretty straight forward "activate the right program in the right order and wait".

But still - the feel and look of the game was pleasing and I had fun playing it. Took me about 8 hours in a slow pace with a cuppa and my back relaxed.

It's hard NOT to compare Hacknet with Uplink though, and if you played Uplink you might feel "locked in" in Hacknet since it's much more streamlined and linear. You can't upgrade your rig, memory, CPU or anything but the hacking is quicker and allows for more typing with autocompletion where Uplink had you clicking and an unhealthy amount of drag-and-drop.

Still, would have been nice if Hacknet had drag-and-drop in the file system. And the ability to make folders.

It's something I really enjoy. It's like real hacking, but easy. I mean, it's not every day that you can go online and crack into Microsoft's (Macrosoft, the "totally originally new company") servers so easily. Honestly, it's not completely Hollywood, but it's also not completely  realistic (of course). The idea of using a Unix-based terminal is actually really cool, and it allows me to brush up on my skills of using such. However, I find it a bit disappointing that there's such a limited RAM, which is now as limited as hard-drive space in--brace yourselves--[i]Uplink[/i]  that there's so little, and for 7.6 hours (as of post) have I not seen any upgrades to it.
The gameplay in this game, however, is captivating. It's hacking: it's tense, it's sweaty, it's chilling: it's everything you'd expect hacking to be, especially once you start getting traced and the beeps start going faster. Now, do I think hacking in this game is OP? No. Do I think it's UP? No. I think hacking in this game is somehow in this uncanny valley of good enough but not enough good. It's, in a sense, "realistic". However, captivating realism isn't the same as slowing down reload speeds.
I find the game in it's fullest, a nice game. It's not the best, and it's not the worst, but for a hack sim, it comes very nicely aligned with--wait for it... [i]Uplink[/i] as a spiritual successor, but not extremely successful. There's limits to the game, of course, games always have that, but personally, it's more story-based with "hack" in the title.

Ever wanted to crack down on some real terminal action to get a peek at what this hacking business is all about? Wonder no more, as Hacknet is here to "teach" you what "hacking" is. 

Immersive, intelligent and just enough unix-commands at your disposal, Hacknet will convince anyone not computer savvy or not paying close enough attention that the things on your monitor sure looks like something you shouldn't be doing, almost like dark wizardry magic. For the most part, the game offers up this illusion at an convincing rate while being beginner-friendly. However, in the world of hacking, there is very little hand holding, so the faster you understand what the ropes are, the better.

To deliver a convincing hacking experience, music is paramount - as Uplink back in the day taught everyone. Here is really delivers, with everything from ambient barrens tunes fit for the breaks between each mission, to serious business from The Algorithm and wildly intense adrenaline pumping Carpenter Brut songs. Hats off, this album is even worth listening to way after you've finished the game. 

As for the the main story, while not top shelf, is interesting enough to keep searching around for clues and getting a better grasp at what's going. As with any self respecting game that depicts hacking, it should have its sheer selectino of surprise elements, and Hacknet doesn't disappoint. However, this is usually found in side missions. The main story should've done more of that as well.

For each time you play, the game changes up names, IPs etc for the nodes to try to keep things sort of fresh, but the missions are mostly the same. All in all, Hacknet is a very solid, albeit simple at times, attempt at creating an immersive, "real enough" hacking simulator that most importantly is -FUN-. The list of unix commands are however at times frustratingly limited, especially if you know what you're doing. Since most of the game is very well laid out in terms of the interface, you start taking it for granted that you should be able to do more than you actually are allowed to. 

For example, "rm file*" will not work since the terminal doesn't support wildcards. Pathing is also needlessly tedious, as it doesn't properly understand using root-nodes in paths. Props however for making it possible to furk up yourself, which is how it should be. Paying attention and going "outside the beaten path" is usually rewarded.
 
Hacknet requires reading and understanding of its core concepts to get the most out of the experience. For those persistent enough, the game also delivers some hilarious content as a nod to the efforts. Here's to hoping the developer makes more content to this game, as the main game is rather short. It'll take you only around 5-6 hours for the main campaign. A multiplayer mode would've been awesome in addition to random missions.

So I loved this game when I first played it, friends would see me scribbling notes pen and paper style (which I recommend) and ask how could I enjoy a game that constantly had me looking like I want to throw something at someone while I was skimming through all the files I could find, but I've never felt more immersed in a game. After my first playthrough I went on a random rampage to get all the achieves followed by wrecking whatever I could get my hands on in game.

Then Labyrinths appeared... I'm not fully through it yet, but what just happened storywise to me. Just made me laugh and angry at the same time, at what happened and I will never be able to recommend this game enough. This game and it's DLC is amazing...
